en: Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into dharma.
It should be understood that those words which are well-known in the world for certain meanings should, when possible, be taken as having those very same meanings in the sūtras;
their meaning is not to be imagined through ellipsis and the like, nor is it to be defined by technical convention.
For in this way, the Vedic sentences themselves are explained by these [works].
Otherwise, both the Vedic sentences would have to be explained, as well as their own constituent word-meanings;
thus, an excessive burden of effort would result.

In this world, this word *atha* is observed to signify the commencement of what follows immediately after what has preceded; yet here, no such preceding matter is perceived. Nevertheless, there must indeed be such a thing.

That being present, the desire to know Dharma becomes possible immediately thereafter; for in this way, it is conceived as having its meaning already well-established. And that is the study of the Veda.
For if that [prior qualification] were present, then that [inquiry] would be possible;
but this is not so.
It is also appropriate for the inquiry into Dharma to follow immediately after any other action.
And even prior to the study of the Veda [it would be possible].
It is replied: however, the Teacher employed the word "atha" (now) with reference to that inquiry into Dharma which is not possible without the study of the Veda.
How so? A manifold investigation of Vedic statements will be undertaken here.
Moreover, we do not at all receive an injunction here prohibiting the inquiry into Dharma prior to the study of the Vedas;
for this single sentence cannot simultaneously prohibit the inquiry into Dharma before the study of the Vedas [and enjoin it after].
Moreover, he will later establish immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

For in that case, the sentence would be split, since the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) here— when it prohibits the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) prior to the study of the Veda— is different from the mode of expression when it teaches immediate succession later on.
In one [interpretation], having studied the Vedas is enjoined while the immediate succession is restated;
in the other, the opposite is the case.
And because the purpose is one, he will state that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
However, once the Veda has been studied, two things present themselves: one must either return from the teacher’s house or investigate the sentences of the Veda.
Regarding this, [the injunction] says: "Do not return from the teacher’s house."
"How indeed should one investigate the Vedic sentences?"— this is the purpose of this instruction.
If this is so, then the study of the Vedas does not precede the inquiry into Dharma.
For thus they hand down the tradition: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath.
And here, one who, having studied the Veda and being about to bathe, should desire to know Dharma, would transgress this sacred tradition (āmnāya).
Now, the sacred tradition is certainly not to be transgressed.
To this it is said: we shall transcend this tradition.
By not transcending it, we would render the Veda—which is actually meaningful—meaningless.
For its purpose is clearly seen to be the instruction regarding ritual action.
Furthermore, the venerable ritualists do not declare that a fruit results from the mere recitation of that [text].

And even as for what they seem to declare, in that case too he will state that it is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), according to the principle: "In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and subordinate rites, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory praise."
Nor is this enjoined as an immediate sequence following the bath for one who has studied the Vedas;
for there is no word here that expresses immediate succession. Indeed, the suffix *ktvā* is traditionally taught to denote priority in time.
It is not in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
For if it were immediate succession, the visible purpose of Vedic study would be contradicted;
rather, this meaning must be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, this bath is not enjoined for the sake of an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Rather, they say that by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the conclusion of the restrictive rules such as the prohibition against bathing occurs simultaneously with the study of the Veda— based on such injunctions as "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe" and "He should not return from the teacher’s house"— precisely in order to avoid the consequence of [the rule] being for an unseen result.
Therefore, the force of the word *atha* is that one should first complete the study of the Veda and only thereafter desire to know Dharma;

we do not say that "the inquiry into Dharma must not be undertaken immediately after any other action," but rather that "having studied the Veda, one should not perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) in haste."
"Immediately thereafter, dharma is to be investigated"—this is the meaning of the word *atha*.
The word *ataḥ* indicates what has preceded by way of a reason (*hetu*), as in: "This country is secure and well-supplied with food..."
"Therefore, I dwell in this region. Likewise, the force of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is: "The Veda has been studied; it is known to be the cause for the desire to know Dharma;
immediately thereafter, Dharma is to be investigated. Thus is the power of the word *ataḥ*.
For one who has not studied the Vedas would be unable to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of Dharma;
therefore, for this reason,
the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is that one should desire to inquire into Dharma immediately thereafter.
The desire to know dharma is "dharma-jijñāsā"; for that is indeed the wish to know it. But how, then, is it to be sought after?
What is the phenomenon? What are its characteristics? What are its means of proof? And what are the fallacious means of proof?
And what is its purpose?

In this regard, the question "What is dharma? and "What are its characteristics? are explained by a single sūtra: "Dharma is a matter characterized by the Vedic injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).
"What are its means of proof, what are the fallacious means of proof,
and what is its ultimate purpose?"— this has been explained by the definition of the "remainder" (śeṣalakṣaṇa). 2.

Where is the supremacy of the Puruṣa, and where is the Puruṣa subordinate to the Guṇas? This aphorism, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), is the summary of these propositions.
Is Dharma well-known or unknown?
If it is well-known, [then...]
It is not something to be investigated;
if it were unestablished, it would be even less so.
Therefore, this section on the inquiry into Dharma is useless.
Alternatively, it is meaningful:
for many learned people are indeed mistaken regarding the Dharma; some declare one thing to be the Dharma, while others declare another.
Some [choose] another;
thus, acting without investigation and adopting just anything at random, one might be frustrated and meet with misfortune.
Therefore, dharma ought to be investigated.
For we maintain that it indeed unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
This is stated as follows:
*Jaimini Sūtra* 1.1.2: Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

They say that *codanā* is a statement that impels one toward action; for it is observed [in common usage] that "I am doing this because I have been urged by my teacher. That by which something is characterized—
The definition of "tallness" is as follows:
they say that smoke is the defining characteristic of fire; by means of that [smoke], that which is defined is [fire].
We maintain that this meaning connects a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known such objects as those that have been, are being, or will be, as well as those that are subtle, concealed, or remote;
no other sense organ is capable of doing so.
But surely, an injunction might state even an object that is not so [as it is], just as any common worldly statement such as, "There are fruits on the riverbank";
for that may also be true.
"It is also false," it is said.
To this it is replied: "To say that one both 'speaks' and is 'false' is a contradiction.
By the term "speaks," it is meant that one causes [another] to understand.
"It becomes the cause for one who is awakening.
And when that which has become the cause exists,
it causes one to awaken.
And if, when there is an injunction, it is understood that "heaven results from the Agnihotra," how can it be said that "it does not happen thus"?
Or, if it does not happen thus, [then the injunction is false].
How is it understood?
To say that one understands a non-existent object is a contradiction.
Furthermore, from the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is not understood with uncertainty such that one might think, "Heaven either comes to be or it does not come to be."
Furthermore, this which is understood with certainty could not be false;
for that cognition which, having arisen, subsequently perishes with the thought "this is not so," is a false cognition.
And this does not undergo reversal at another time, in another person, in another state, or in another place;
therefore, it is non-false.
As for that which is worldly speech, however—
If that [information] comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses,
it is indeed non-false;
however, if it comes from an untrustworthy person or concerns an object beyond the senses, [it is otherwise].
That [knowledge] originates from human intellect and is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
for it is impossible for a person to know it without [relying on] a verbal testimony.
If it is argued that it is understood from another human verbal testimony, [the response follows].
That too is equal to that [previous case].
In matters of this kind, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge,
just as the word of those born blind does not regarding specific forms of color.
— But surely, instruction is not possible for those who are ignorant;
yet Manu and others have indeed given instruction. Therefore, these persons must have been existent and must have possessed knowledge.
Just as it is understood from the very fact of seeing that "form is perceived by the eye"—it is said in reply:
for instruction may arise even from delusion;
and when there is no delusion, it may likewise arise from the Veda.
Moreover, from a human statement, there arises the cognition, "This person knows it thus," but not the cognition, "The object is thus.
Furthermore, the cognition derived from a statement composed by a human being can indeed be subverted.
But there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic word.
[Objection: There will be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*);
having observed that human speech is false, it is inferred that the Vedic word is false because of its commonality as "speech."
No, because they are distinct.
For it is not possible that when one thing is false, another thing should also be false, precisely because they are distinct.

For the dark complexion of Devadatta does not necessarily imply that Yajñadatta must also be dark. Furthermore, the inference that the Vedic word is false because it shares the same nature as human speech is contradicted by the direct perception of conviction regarding the Vedic word.
Furthermore, inference that contradicts perception cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*).
If this is so, then that which brings about the highest good must be investigated.
"What is the use of an inquiry into Dharma?
It is replied: that alone which brings about the highest good is denoted by the word "Dharma."
How is this understood? For indeed, those who perform a sacrifice are designated as "righteous" (dhārmika).
And whoever is the agent of something is designated by that [action],
as for example, "a cooker" or "a reaper."
Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is alone denoted by the word "dharma," not only in common worldly usage but also in the Veda.
The gods sacrificed the sacrifice with the sacrifice;
those were the first dharmas.
Thus, they teach that dharma is precisely what is denoted by the word "sacrifice" (yajati). Here, both are indicated by the injunction (codanā):
the beneficial and the harmful. What is the beneficial?
—that which, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, leads to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
What is "non-benefit" (anartha)?—that which leads to transgression (pratyavāya), such as the Śyena, the Vajra, the Iṣu, and so forth.
In that context, the term "benefit" (artha) is included so that dharma which is non-beneficial might not be [mistakenly] designated as dharma.
But how is this an evil?
For it is violence, and that is prohibited.
But how can an evil be taught as something to be done?
It is said: the hawk-sacrifice and the like are not understood as things to be performed;
for their instruction is to the effect that "this is the means for one who wishes to kill."
For they recite: "One practicing malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena," and not "Malevolent magic should be practiced.
But surely this sūtra is incapable of expressing these two meanings?
Dharma is characterized by injunction (*codanā*), not by the senses and so forth;
and dharma is that which is beneficial, not that which is harmful.
For this is a single sentence.
If that were so, there would be a contradiction.
It is replied: this applies only where the meaning is understood from the sentence itself;
and that is the case with Vedic texts, not with the Sūtras.
When a meaning is understood from elsewhere, it is recognized that the *sūtra* has such a meaning; and because a portion [of that meaning] is formulated as a *sūtra*, it is called a *sūtra*.
In this regard, it should be understood that these two are portions of two distinct sentences.
Alternatively, since it is stated that dharma-ness belongs to an existing object characterized by Vedic injunction, the two statements have the same meaning.
Jaimini 1.1.3: "The investigation of its means of knowledge."
We have stated that "the knowledge of dharma has its source in injunction" (codanā).
That was stated as a mere proposition;
now we shall examine its source.
Is it only *codanā* (an injunction), or is there something else as well?
Therefore, it is not yet determined that "Dharma is a matter characterized by *codanā*.
To this, it is said:

Jaimini 1.1.4: When there is contact of a person's sense organs with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception; it is not a means [of knowing Dharma], because it consists in the apprehension of what is already present.
This is now examined:
first of all, direct perception is not a cause [for knowing the Dharma].
What is the reason?
For its definition is as follows:
when there is contact of a person’s sense organs with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That cognition which arises for a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and the object—[is perception].
That is perception; and this object, being future, does not exist at the time of the cognition.
Furthermore, this apprehension is of what exists, not of what does not exist.
Therefore, perception is not the cause [of dharma].
This sutra is not intended to determine any one among these—whether it be cognition, birth, or contact;
rather, it means that when there is a conjunction of the sense organ and the object, [perception arises].
It is determined only that [the object] does not exist;
for if more than one [negation] were determined, the sentence would be split.
Furthermore, because inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony are preceded by perception, they too lack causal efficacy [in this context].
Nor is it non-existence;
for [Jaimini 1.1.5 states]: "But the connection of a word with its meaning is innate; its cognition is instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an object not perceived [by other means];
that is the authority of Bādarāyaṇa."
Because of its independence.
By "autpattika" (inborn), we mean "eternal.
For "origination" (utpatti) is used figuratively to denote "existence" (bhāva). The existence of word and meaning is inseparable from their relationship.
There is no subsequent connection between two things that have already arisen;

rather, the innate relationship between a word and its meaning is the means of cognizing that dharma characterized by the *agnihotra* and other such rites, which is not apprehended through perception or other ordinary means of knowledge.
How so? Because there exists an authoritative instruction (*upadeśa*).
"Instruction" (upadeśa) is the utterance of a specific word;
and that knowledge is non-deviant,
for once that knowledge has arisen, it does not turn out to be erroneous.
Furthermore, when a cognition has arisen that is not erroneous,
it cannot be said,
"This is not so," in accordance with how it is cognized.
"It is not so; it is not as this is not understood, but rather it is thus."
One thing would be in his heart, while another would be in his speech;
thus, from such a speaker, this contradiction is understood: "it both exists and does not exist."
Therefore, that is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because it is independent;
for this being the case, no other cognition or another person need be depended upon.
For this is a matter of personal conviction; Bādarāyaṇa’s opinion is being stated here in order to honor Bādarāyaṇa,
not to reject his own view.

The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), however, explained this passage beginning with "the investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*) in a different manner: "The cause need not be examined;
for perception and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are well-established, and the scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them."
Therefore, that too should not be examined.
[Objection: Surely the cause (nimitta) must be examined because of deviation;
for instance, mother-of-pearl appears as if it were silver.
Therefore, it contradicts direct perception, and because it is rooted in that [perception], it also contradicts inference and the other means of knowledge.
One who acts without examining these may, as a consequence, be frustrated in their purpose and sometimes incur misfortune.
This is not so;
that which is perceptual does not deviate from reality.
That which deviates is not perception.
What, then, is perception?
Jaimini 1.1.4a: When there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is true perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*).
When a cognition has a certain object as its domain, the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs upon contact with that very object is true perception.
When a cognition has one object as its domain while occurring during contact with another, that is not perception.
But how, then, is it understood that "this [cognition] occurs during contact with that [object]"?
Is this [the case] when there is association with another?
That which does not involve association with another involves association with that very thing.
The opposite of this is "contact with something else.
How is this known?
For when one perceives even a mother-of-pearl shell as silver, one thinks, "My eye is in contact with silver."
For where a subverting cognition arises— such as "this is not so;
this is a false cognition"—
that occurs when there is contact with something other [than the object perceived].
"That [cognition] is erroneous because of its association [with a false object]"—
how is this understood prior to the arising of a subverting cognition,
when at that time there is no distinction whatsoever between a correct cognition and a false cognition?
When the mind is afflicted by hunger and the like, or when a sense faculty is impaired by cataracts and the like, or when an external object is characterized by subtlety and so forth—
From that arises false knowledge,
whereas when [the senses] are unimpaired, right knowledge arises;
for the contact between the sense organs, the mind, and the object is indeed the cause of knowledge.
In its absence, due to ignorance,
the defect inherent therein becomes the cause of false cognition.
For knowledge regarding those who are defective is indeed false.
How is this understood?
Because correct cognition is observed when the defects have been removed.
If it is asked, "How is the presence or absence of defects understood?"—

we would consider [the scripture] to be free from defects on the grounds that there is a lack of evidence for defects, provided that we do not perceive any defect even when searching with diligent effort.
Therefore, that cognition alone is incorrect for which the instrument is defective and for which there is the conviction "this is false," and no other.
[Objection: But surely every cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream?
For it is observed that the nature of a cognition is to be without an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*), as in a dream;
even for one who is awake, there occurs a cognition such as "a pillar" or "a wall.
Therefore, that too is without an objective basis.
It is said: How could the cognition of one who is awake, which is extremely well-ascertained as "this is a pillar," ever be erroneous?
If it is argued that even in a dream, the cognition was likewise extremely well-ascertained prior to waking, and thus there is no difference between the two cases—
"No, because in a dream there is the perception of error, whereas in the other state there is no error.
If it is argued that "because of the similarity between them, this will also be the case for the other," [we reply: no.
If the falsity of a dream-cognition is due to its being a cognition,
then it must also apply to a waking cognition.
Alternatively, if the cause of such [falsity] is the very nature of the cognition itself, [then it applies equally to all].
It cannot be said that "this [dream cognition] is different from other cognitions" on account of its being a cognition;
rather, the falsity of dream-cognition is understood through its contrast with the opposite case.
If one asks, "Why?"—
Due to the weakness of the mind when accompanied by sleep, sleep is the cause of false states at the beginning and end of dreams;
for one who is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there is simply an absence of cognitive objects,
for it is said that "one who is in deep sleep is indeed not cognizing."
Therefore, the cognition of one who is awake is not false.
But surely, could there not be a defect in the instruments even for one who is awake? If there were such a defect, it would be perceived.
If it is argued that [the dream] is not understood even at the time of seeing the dream, that is not so;
for upon waking, one understands: "My mind was overcome by sleep."
But it is empty. How so?
We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition;
moreover, our cognition is directly perceived.
Therefore, we observe that there is no such thing as an objective form distinct from that [cognition].
This might indeed be so, provided that cognition possessed the form of the object.
But for us, cognition is formless,
while the external object possesses form;
for that [object] is perceived through direct perception as connected with external space.
For perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain;
for that [cognition] is momentary and will not persist until the time of another cognition.
If it were argued that "this [cognition], while itself arising, is known and makes another object known, like a lamp," that is not so.
For no one perceives cognition with respect to an object that is unknown;
rather, once it is known, one understands it through inference. In that case, simultaneity is untenable.
— But surely, an object is said to be "known" only when cognition has already arisen, not when it has not yet arisen;
therefore, cognition arises first, and the object is known afterwards.
— True.
First the cognition arises,
but it is not first known.
For it sometimes happens that an object which is known is called "unknown";
moreover, there is no perception of the form of a cognition apart from the designation of its object.
Therefore, cognition is not inexpressible, and for us, that which is inexpressible is perception;
thus, cognition is not perceptible.
Moreover, even if there were a single form, it would be the non-existence of cognition itself,
and not of the object which is actually perceived;
yet, there is no such single form.
For we infer cognition to be indeed formless, whereas we apprehend the object as possessing form through direct perception;
therefore, cognition has the object as its objective support.
Moreover, the cognition of a cloth occurs only when threads are appropriated as its specific cause;
otherwise, even when threads are appropriated, a person with unimpaired faculties might sometimes have the notion of a jar.
But such is not the case.

Therefore, cognition is not without an objective basis; hence, perception does not err. Inference is the cognition of an object not present to the senses, arising from the observation of one part of a known relationship.

That [inference] is of two kinds: that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*) and that based on a relationship perceived through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).
Among these, an example of that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation is the cognition of the form of fire resulting from the sight of the form of smoke.

An example of that based on a relationship perceived through generalization is the recollection of motion in the sun, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by motion.
Scripture is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of words.
Analogy also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] through similarity,
just as the sight of a gavaya produces the recollection of a cow.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact because a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for;
for example, the postulation of Devadatta’s presence outside—though unperceived—upon seeing that he, who is alive, is absent from his house.
Non-existence (*abhāva*) is likewise the absence of a means of valid cognition, regarding an object not in contact with the senses, such as the fact that "it does not exist."
Therefore, because it is well-established, its cause need not be investigated.
Now, let it be granted that perception and the other [means of knowledge] are indeed valid means of cognition;
however, verbal testimony (śabda) is not a valid means of cognition. Why?
Jaimini 1.1.4b: [The Veda] is not without a basis, because it is the perception of things that actually exist.
Sound is signless and immeasurable;
for that which is an object of perception but is not perceived does not exist.
Just as the horn of a hare [is non-existent],
so too are the sense organs the means of perception for cattle and other such beings;
yet, following the sacrifice intended to obtain cattle, cattle are not perceived.
Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit;
and at the time of the action, there must be the fruit of the action.
For at the very time of the crushing, [the result occurs].
If it is argued that there is pleasure from massaging at that time, but it will yield its fruit at a later time—
no.
We understand that the fruit of the sacrifice is not [obtained] at a later time.
Why? Because when that [sacrifice] existed, it did not bestow the fruit.
When the fruit arises, that [cause] no longer exists;
and being non-existent, how could it give?
Moreover, the result is heard as occurring at the very time of the action;
this is understood from the statement, "The sacrifice is the instrument," for if the instrument has already arisen, [the result must follow].
"An effect must exist.
Yet we perceive another cause for the result directly before our eyes;
and when a visible cause exists, it is not possible to postulate an invisible one.
Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge [to establish it].
Thus, we consider that even such results as heaven cannot belong to the Veda, since its transgressions have been observed. Furthermore, some Vedic statement is even contradicted by what is perceived.

Having prescribed the piling of the sacrificial vessels, [the scripture] says: "This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world. Thus it designates the visible body [as the agent].
Yet that [body] does not go to the heavenly world, for it is visibly seen being burned.
Furthermore, this term "goes" (*yāti*) is not an injunctive word;
and a statement of this kind that contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is invalid, just like the sayings: "Gourd-bottles sink in water" or "Stones float."
Because of that similarity, there would also be a lack of confidence in the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites.
Therefore, dharma is not an object characterized by injunction.
[Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5a: Rather, the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; from that, knowledge [of dharma arises].
The word "tu" (but) excludes that which is cooked [or produced].

The relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya); it is the cognition of that object characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth, which is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge. And thus, it is said: "Right cognition is characterized by the Vedic injunction (codanā)."
For if the relationship were of human origin,
one might suspect that the cognition [arising from it] is false;
for in that case, it would be dependent upon another's cognition.
Now, if it is asked how the word can be false when it speaks,
[the answer is that] at that time there is no comprehension from any other person;
for when it is said "it speaks," it means "it causes one to understand."
"It becomes a cause for one who is awakening.
If he awakens by himself when the sound has become the cause,
how could he say, deceived as he is, "This is not so"?
Nor does it produce a doubtful cognition such as, "Whether this [injunction] exists or not";
nor does there arise, at another time, in another place, in another state, or in relation to another person, a further cognition that cannot be designated as "this is false.
Furthermore, even when an inferential cognition arises—based on observing the subversion of other cognitions—thinking, "In this case too, [the cognition] will be subverted," [it does not occur].
That [notion] too, being contradicted by this perceptual cognition, is sublated.
Therefore, dharma is indeed characterized solely by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
This might be so:
There is no connection whatsoever between a word and its object;
how then could it be either human-made or not human-made?
Why so? Because if there were a connection with the object, [it would follow that the word is produced by someone].

If it were intended that the relationship [between word and object] is characterized by conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (*kṣura*) and "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), there would follow the cutting and the filling of the mouth respectively;
however, other types of relationships— such as those of cause and effect, sign and signified, substratum and superstratum, or sexual union— are simply untenable in the case of a word.
It is said: You do not point out that single relationship which is to be designated here— that relationship between the signifier and the signified characterized as the name and the named.
He asks: "If a word is expressive, why does it not express its meaning when heard for the first time?
It is replied: "In all cases, our observation is the authority."

For we understand that [the word] is "indicative" (*pratyāyaka*) upon seeing its cognition (*pratyaya*), but not when first heard, because no cognition is seen at the time of the first hearing; rather, it becomes so through being heard as many times as it takes for [the cognition to arise], such that one recognizes: "This is the name."
When it is determined that "this one possesses perception," then comprehension of the meaning arises from what has been heard so many times;
just as the eye, though not a seer, does not fail to see because it does not illuminate without external light.
If [the word] heard for the first time does not cause comprehension, then the relationship between the word and its object must be something produced.
Why? Because by their very nature, these two—the word and the object—are unrelated.
For we perceive the word in the mouth and the object on the ground;
"this is the word, not the object."
They designate it thus: "This is the meaning, not the word.
There is also a difference in form:
they utter this word, "cow" (gaur).
They understand the object as possessing a dewlap and so forth;
and whatever relation exists between two distinct entities is observed to be produced.
As in the case of the rope and the jar.
Now, what is the word here in the expression "cow" (*gaur*)?
The venerable Upavarṣa says: "The phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga."
For in common worldly usage, the term "word" (śabda) is well-known to refer to an object apprehended by the sense of hearing;
and those [phonemes] are indeed apprehended by the sense of hearing.
If this is so, then the cognition of meaning is not possible.
How so? For when each individual syllable is cognized, the meaning is not apprehended;
nor does there exist any other entity called a "collection" apart from the syllables from which the comprehension of meaning could arise.
For when there is the sound *ga*, there are not at that time the sound *au* and the visarga;
and when there are the sound *au* and the visarga, [there is not the sound *ga*].
At that time, it is not the letter *ga*;
therefore, there exists another word "go" distinct from the letters *ga* and so forth, from which the comprehension of meaning would arise.
If it is argued that the meaning is understood through recollection even when the sound has disappeared, we say no;
for since recollection is also momentary, it is equal to the syllables [in this regard].
There is no fault, however, in the view that the final syllable, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding syllables, is what conveys the meaning.
But even so, would not the common worldly expression, "We understand the meaning from the word," be untenable?
It is said: if it is untenable, then let it be untenable.

For a worldly statement cannot be accepted as authoritative merely because it is not logically consistent; an object that is not apprehended through perception and other means of valid cognition cannot be established on that basis alone.
Indeed, we observe that worldly statements are both those whose meanings are consistent and those whose meanings are inconsistent, such as:
"Devadatta,..."
Examples include such phrases as "Bring the cow" (*gām abhyāja*) and so forth, as well as "Ten pomegranates, six cakes" (*daśa dāḍimāni ṣaḍ apūpāḥ*) and so forth.

But surely even the authors of the treatises have said this: "One expresses an action consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages by means of a verb (*ākhyāta*), such as 'he goes' (*vrajati*) or 'he cooks' (*pacati*), [covering] from the beginning until its completion. Just so.
Even the words of the author of a treatise are not sufficient to establish this matter as being without authority;
moreover, it is not at all the case that its meaning is untenable: from the syllables arises the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Since the comprehension of meaning arises from the linguistic formation (*saṃskāra*), syllables serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for that comprehension of meaning.
If it is argued that this term [“cause”] is used figuratively, we reply:
no, the status of being a cause in respect to syllables is not figurative.
Because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, and does not exist when that is absent;
furthermore, even if [the term] were figurative,
one cannot postulate an object not apprehended by perception and the other means of knowledge merely on the grounds that "a figurative word must not be used."

For when it is said, "The boy is fire," one does not conclude that "the boy is indeed the flame" just so that the word "fire" might not be taken figuratively. Nor is the word "cow" perceived as something distinct from the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and so on,
because no difference is observed and because non-difference is observed.
For the phonemes beginning with *ga* are directly perceived;
therefore, the word "cow" (*gaur*), which begins with *ga* and ends with the visarga, consists of nothing but these syllables. There is no other entity called a "word" distinct from them.
[Objection: But surely, even in the hypothesis of a *saṃskāra* (mental impression), there is the postulation of something unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
[Reply: It is said: in the hypothesis of a word (*śabda*), there would be both that [postulation of the *saṃskāra*] and the postulation of the word itself.
Therefore, the word is nothing other than the phonemes (*akṣara*).
Now, what is the meaning of this word "cow"?
We say it is the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth.
But is it not the case that the existence of such a form is yet to be proven, or does it not exist at all?
Being directly perceived, it cannot be something to be proven;
for indeed, "the rucaka," "the svastika," and "the vardhamānaka" are seen through direct perception.
If it is argued that this is a delusion (*vyāmoha*), we say no;
for one cannot speak of "delusion" unless there is a subversion of cognition (*pratyayaviparyāsa*).
Even in the absence of a distinct external object of such a kind, a cognition arises, such as "a row."
If it is argued that [the examples] are "a herd" and "a forest," we say no;
this statement you have introduced is incoherent.

Is it the case that direct perception itself is being subverted by the claim, "When the forest does not exist, how can there be a cognition of the forest? by asserting that "even the trees do not exist"?
If this is so, then that Mahāyāna position has been refuted.
Or rather, is the proponent of the existence of the universal form (ākṛti) being censured because another established doctrine of yours is flawed?
"Even when a forest does not exist, the cognition of a forest would follow.
Even so, those who are unable to refute the matter at hand fall into the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by refuting another established doctrine, because that [refutation] is not a proof.
For he will say: "Let it be flawed if it is flawed;
what does it matter whether that which is under discussion is proven by you to be flawed or unflawed, or whether my own position is refuted?"

And since no forest is perceived apart from the trees, it is understood that "the forest does not exist. If, however, with respect to the forest, a cognition contrary to its existence should arise due to some other cause, [then it would be otherwise].
Because this cognition of a forest is false, we understand that "the forest does not exist.
However, the cognition regarding cows and the like does not undergo subversion;
therefore, there is a disparity. Now, [if you argue...]
In the case of forests and the like, there is no subversion of cognition,
nor is it the case that "they do not exist.
Therefore, the comparison with a forest as a row [of trees] is irrelevant.
Therefore, Jaimini’s statement that "the word-meaning is the form (ākṛti)" is established.
And how the form is the meaning of a word, we shall demonstrate more precisely below.
Now, what is this "relation"?
It is that when the word is cognized, the object is cognized.
However, it has been previously established that this [relation] is produced.
Therefore, we think that the Vedas were composed by some person who established a relationship between words and their meanings in order to facilitate worldly communication.
To this, it is now replied:
"Because the relationship is not of human origin, [the Veda] is established [as authoritative]."
But how is it understood that "this relationship is not of human origin"?
Because of the non-existence of a person who could establish the relationship. How is it that there is no such person?
Because direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is absent, and because the others are preceded by it; [one might object:

"Surely, due to having occurred long ago, [the Veda] would not be an object for those of the present day. [We reply: It is not the case that something which has occurred long ago would not be remembered.
Furthermore, non-remembrance [of the connection] cannot occur in places such as the Himalayas in the same manner as it does for wells or groves;
for while there may be a separation from persons in those places due to the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage,
there is no separation of persons from the linguistic usage of words and their meanings.
—It might be argued: "People who deal with the mere relationship [of word and meaning], disregarding the recollection of an author as being useless, might forget it. —That is not so;
for if a person, having created the relationship, were to cause it to be used in practice, [then such a recollection would be necessary].
It must necessarily be remembered at the time of legal procedure;
for when there is agreement between the doer and the transactor, the purpose is accomplished, but not when there is disagreement.
For indeed, by the word "vṛddhi," the vowels ā, ai, and au would not be understood through common usage by one who is not a follower of Pāṇini, nor by one who does not accept Pāṇini’s composition.

Likewise, even by the letter *m*, a group of three syllables consisting entirely of heavy (*guru*) syllables would not be recognized by one who is not a follower of Piṅgala, nor by one who does not accept Piṅgala’s composition.
Therefore, the author and the user must reach a mutual agreement.
Therefore, by those who employ the Vedas, the author of the relationship [between word and meaning] and of the linguistic usage must necessarily be remembered;
for if the author of the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" were forgotten, nothing at all would be understood from the rule "vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham."

Therefore, from this lack of recollection, we understand that "the Vedas were not composed by anyone for the sake of linguistic usage after establishing a [conventional] relationship [between word and meaning].
Even if such forgetfulness were possible, nevertheless, we could not establish an author of the relationship without some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as we do not accept the existence of a rabbit’s horn merely on the grounds that "even an existing thing may be unperceived" without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
so too [we cannot conclude] that the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (eternal).
But surely, one might object, we could establish the existence of such a relator through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
For we do not observe anyone comprehending a meaning from a word with which no connection has been established; if they were so to comprehend it,
they would do so even upon hearing it for the first time.
If it is argued that because that [connection] is not perceived, there must necessarily be a relator, we say: no;
because the instruction is given as an established fact. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5b)
If objects were not apprehended necessarily due to the absence of a creator of the relationship, then we would understand the creator of the relationship through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
However, there is another way.
It is observed that children, while listening to elders engaged in transactions for their own purposes, come to understand the meaning through direct perception.
Those elders, too, when they were children, [understood it] from other elders.
Or it might be that they [the relations] also [derive] from others, and thus there is no beginning;
or else, not even a single word was ever connected with its meaning, but rather the relations were established by someone at some point.

In this case, since there is the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), one does not arrive at the existence of an author of the relationship by implication. Furthermore, those who maintain that the relationship is based on the usage of elders point to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whereas others postulate an author of the relationship.
Furthermore, when perception stands as an adversary, conceptual construction is not tenable;
therefore, there is an absence of a relationship [between word and object].
And there is no deviation [of the word from its object]. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5c)
Just as the word "cow" applies to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth in this region, so it is in all difficult places;
how could many establishers of the relationship ever come together?
Not even one [of them] would be able [to do so];
therefore, there is no connection.
Another says:
And there is no deviation.
For there is no time whatsoever distinct from the act of relationship in which not even a single word was related to any meaning.
Why? Because the very act of establishing a relationship is not possible [at such a time].
Necessarily, this [relation] must be established by some word;
and by what has it been established for that [word] by which it is established?
If it were created by someone else,
then for that person one would ask "by whom?
and for him "by whom?"— thus there would be no finality.

Therefore, one who necessarily establishes this relationship must admit that there are certain words whose relationship [to their meanings] is already established through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
If such establishment through usage exists, then there is no logical necessity for a [new] relationship to exist; thus, even presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) does not apply.
—It might be argued: "How do children, whose connection [to the meaning] is not yet established, understand from the elders?
—Indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is observed;
for we see children actually understanding from the elders.
But it is not the case that those who have not apprehended the relationship [of words] are the makers of that relationship;
therefore, there is a disparity.
Jaimini 1.1.5d: "When the object is unperceived..."
Furthermore, regarding an object such as a deity that is not perceived, the creation of a name is both purposeless and impossible;

for names are created in order to comprehend specific distinctions and with reference to those specific distinctions. Since those specific distinctions are not known, both [of these purposes] are unattainable.
Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is not of human origin; and for this reason, it is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Jaimini 1.1.5d: "That [Veda] is authoritative."
Because of its independence.
For this being the case, it does not depend upon another person or another means of cognition.
Therefore, dharma is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (codanā) and not by any other characteristic.
The mention of Bādarāyaṇa has already been explained.
Now, as for what was said—"Sound is without a cause;

because no fruit is seen at the time of the action, and because the action is absent at a later time, there is no means of valid cognition"—to that it is replied: It would not be a means of valid cognition.
If there were only five means of valid cognition,
then whatever is used to cognize something would itself be a means of valid cognition.
An object is also cognized through verbal testimony;
therefore, verbal testimony is also a means of valid cognition, just like perception.
Nor does something become uncomprehended merely because it is not comprehended by one means of valid cognition while being comprehended by another;
nor is it heard in scripture that "once the action has been performed, the fruit arises at that very moment."
However, as for the statement that "the fruit is obtained through karma," and the claim that "there exists another perceptible cause for the fruit at a later time," this is not a fault.
And that is indeed the reason there, as well as the word itself.

As for the statement presented which contradicts perception—namely, "This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world," which designates the perceptible body as such—it is said in reply: because of its connection with the body.
He who possesses that body is also called "the one equipped with sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhin*) by virtue of those sacrificial implements.
He asks: who is this other?
"We do not perceive him."—
"But surely we perceive him by means of the vital breaths and so forth;
he who is the agent of such activities as breathing out, breathing in, inhaling, winking, and so on."
Thus, he is "the possessor of sacrificial implements" in this body.
But is it not the case that the body itself breathes in and breathes out?
No; for the vital breaths and so forth are not qualities of the body.
For they possess properties different from those of the body,
because they do not persist as long as the body does;
for as long as the body exists, its qualities such as form (rūpa) and so forth remain.
However, vital breath and the other [functions] do not exist even when the body is present;
therefore, vital breath and the others are not qualities of the body.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are perceived by themselves.
Unlike color and other qualities, [the self] is not perceived by another even as a quality of the body.
Therefore, because it possesses characteristics different from the qualities of the body, that which possesses the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhin*) is distinct from the body.
[The opponent] asks: "From what source is this conviction derived that there exists a possessor of those [qualities] such as pleasure, who is distinct from them?"
For we do not perceive its essential nature apart from pleasure and the rest;
therefore, it does not exist, like the horn of a hare.
If it is argued: "Of what would there be pleasure and the rest without that [self]?"
We shall say that it belongs to no one at all;
for it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a related possessor.
When both the relation and the related entity are perceived, it is understood that "this is the related entity of that.
For indeed, having perceived the moon or the sun, one does not search for another related entity by asking, "To whom does this belong?"

It is determined that [the self] belongs to no one at all; therefore, there is no possessor of pleasure and so forth other than those very states themselves. Alternatively, if something has been perceived, its correlate must necessarily be postulated.
—Then, having perceived the self in this manner, we would search for another related entity, asking, "To whom does this belong?
Having postulated that one, and having postulated yet another, there would be an infinite regress.
Now, if you were to postulate some [entity] and not postulate any further related entity, you would stop right there and be satisfied with that alone.
Therefore, being fully satisfied with consciousness alone, you ought to rest there.
To this it is replied: if there is no knower other than consciousness, then who is it that is said to "know"?
The designation of a knower is established by this word;
therefore, we shall postulate a self distinct from cognition so that this word may be meaningful.
He says: "The gods will make this word meaningful."
If they think that [the self] must be conceptualized,
then indeed many people here who assert the existence of a self— saying "there is a self, there is a self"— become direct speakers of that very word which proclaims the existence of a self.
Nevertheless, they are not even able to postulate the existence of a self,
much less [assert] that it "knows," given the observation of the indirect term [used in such a way].
Therefore, this is incorrect.
It is said: we perceive the self through desire.
How so? For desire arises toward an object previously perceived and intended, not toward one never before perceived.
Just as there is no desire for us regarding those sweet tree fruits to the north of Mount Meru which have never before been perceived by those of our own kind, so too,
even when an object has been perceived by one person, there is no desire for it in another who has not perceived it.
Furthermore, there arises on one day a desire for that which was perceived on another day;
therefore, we understand that this [desire] has the same agent as that perception.
If this perceiver were merely consciousness alone, [the desire would not arise].
If that [consciousness] were destroyed, on what other day could there be a desire?
Furthermore, if the knower were eternal and distinct from consciousness, then he who was the perceiver on one day—
"On the following day as well, he alone will seek [it];
otherwise, the desire would be impossible.
To this, he says: "Where do we have the conviction that it is impossible?"
That which is not apprehended by a means of valid cognition—
we do not perceive anything other than consciousness; and that which we do not perceive, [does not exist].
We understand that this [object] does not exist at all, just like a hare's horn;
yet, even in its absence, the existence of consciousness is not untenable,
precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception.
And its momentariness is established by perception itself.
Furthermore, if there were no knower other than consciousness, and if consciousness were impermanent, then desire on a subsequent day would be untenable;
yet this is not so, precisely because it is apprehended through perception.
Indeed, it has never been observed that "the very one who perceives on one day is the very same one who desires on the next day.
However, this has been observed: that in some cases, one person desires what was seen by another.
"In some cases it is not so; one person desires [a result] within the same continuum, but does not desire it in another continuum.
Therefore, there is no other [self] distinct from pleasure and the rest.
To this it is replied: It is not tenable to say, "Those who do not remember [the object] desire [it]. Nor does memory arise with respect to what was never previously perceived.
Therefore, memory is untenable within a mere aggregate of consciousness that is momentary.
Here it is said: Memory, like desire, is defined as a cognition similar to a previous cognition, or a cognition having the previous cognition as its object.
And that is not impossible, even if the seer has perished, since it arises on a subsequent day.
Precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception:
the cognition that one mass of aggregates has of another mass of aggregates is perceived by another [cognition] born of that same continuum, but not by one born of a different continuum.
Therefore, the aggregates (skandhas) are empty. Now, regarding this point, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"This mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes along with them."
“There is no consciousness after death.
To this it is said: this is not so;
for when something was seen on one day, there arises on another day the cognition, “I saw this.”
And this occurs with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), not with respect to another;
for that [other] is indeed someone who saw on a previous day.
Therefore, there exists another distinct from that [self].
Regarding this word "I":
it is said that the word "I" is also seen used figuratively for another, as in: "I myself am the son."
"I myself am Devadatta;
I myself am going"—to this it is said: we do not designate the word "I," when it is being employed, as a reason for any other referent.
Rather, we recognize a cognition of re-identification that is distinct from the word itself;
for we perceive this fact: "We ourselves perceived this object on another day, and we ourselves remember it today."
Therefore, we understand this matter thus: "We ourselves were yesterday, and we ourselves are today.
And those who were yesterday and today—
They have not perished;
moreover, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage which, having introduced the subject with "This self, indeed, is indestructible," declares: "It is unbreakable, for it cannot be broken."
Likewise, [it is said]: "Verily, this self is indestructible and of an imperishable nature," whereas consciousness is perishable;
therefore, we understand that it is other than what is perishable.
And it is not possible to understand it in this way: "Objects do not exist in the manner that they are perceived; rather, they exist in the manner that they are not perceived.
For if that were so, [it would follow that] "the rabbit does not exist," [and yet its horns are perceived].
One might understand that "the horn of a rabbit exists";
nor can it be said that the cognition of "I" is an illusion, because there is no subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) to contradict it.
Therefore, there exists [the self] distinct from pleasure and the other [feelings].
If this is so, then that very [self] is designated as "the possessor of sacrificial implements.
He said: "If there is a knower other than consciousness,"
Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be demonstrated as "this is it" or "it is such-and-such.
But it is not so demonstrated;
therefore, there is nothing other than that [consciousness].
To this it is replied: it is self-cognizable;
it cannot be seen by another. How, then, could it be demonstrated?

Just as a certain person with sight perceives form for himself but cannot demonstrate it to another who is blind from birth, and yet one does not conclude that "it does not exist" merely because it cannot be demonstrated to another— so too this person perceives the self for himself, yet he is unable to show it to another.
Because another observer lacks the power of vision with respect to that person,
that other person also perceives only his own self, not the self of another.
Therefore, all [beings] indeed exist, perceiving themselves by their own respective selves, even though they are not perceived by other persons.
Regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "When speech has become silent, what light does this person have?"
"It is the light of the Self, O Emperor," he said.
Regarding the point that it is not perceived by another, there is also this Brāhmaṇa passage: "It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped."
This is intended to mean that [the self] is not grasped by another. Why? Because of the statement regarding its being self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*).
On this point as well, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "In this state, this person..."
“He becomes his own light.
But by what means is this told to another?
Regarding that means as well, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: “This Self is ‘not this, not this’; thus he said.”
This [self] cannot be pointed out by saying, "It is of such a form";
rather, the means of instruction for it is the negation of whatever another perceives.
Another person perceives the body;
by means of that, the self is taught:
"The body is not the self."
By the negation of the body, it is taught that "there exists a self (ātman) other than the body.
Likewise, by the negation of [the claim] that the vital breaths and so forth are the self, that which is other than them is taught.
Similarly, pleasures and so forth residing in another are perceived by another through their indicative marks (liṅga).
Since those [aggregates] are also not the self, that which is other than them is taught by way of their negation;
and the fact that one who sees for himself is not other than that [self] is also inferred from the activity of the person (puruṣa).

When that person exerts himself on the previous day toward the completion of tasks half-finished and the performance of remaining duties, it is understood from his activity: "Surely he perceives the impermanent as permanent.
And this is also taught through analogy: "Just as you yourself perceive yourself,"
By this analogy, understand that "I too see it in exactly the same way," just as someone might describe their own sensation to another, saying, "It is as if I am being burned;
it is as if I am being driven away."
"It is as if I am being obstructed.
Therefore, because it is understood by itself, there exists a person distinct from that [consciousness].
As for what is also said, "Setting aside consciousness, let that [person] be pointed out," [it is replied:]...
If you negate the means itself, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means;
for this is precisely the method by which objects to be known are to be known: "in whatever manner something is known..."
He said, "It is so.
For example: "What is that which is called white?
"That in which whiteness exists."
“What is that which is called ‘whiteness’? “It is that wherein the word ‘white’ is applied. “Where is its application?”
"That which is understood when the word 'white' is uttered"—
therefore, it is impossible to demonstrate the form of anything by setting aside consciousness.
Nor does the meaning of a cognition necessarily become understood simply because the cognition itself is apprehended.
For even when the cognition is not itself perceived, the object is indeed perceived;
indeed, it has already been stated previously that it is not the consciousness that is perceptible, but rather the object to be known that is perceptible.
If one must deny [the self], then one may as well deny consciousness rather than the object; this has already been stated.
Therefore, there exists a permanent person (puruṣa) distinct from pleasure and the rest.
Now, as for what was said: "A mass of consciousness alone, arising from these elements, perishes after them..."

Regarding the statement, "There is no consciousness after death," it is said in reply: "Right here, the Blessed One has led me into the depths of confusion. Following this objection, [the Buddha] denied that his words were intended to lead one into confusion and explained them thus: "O Vāseṭṭha, I do not speak of confusion."
"Indeed, this self is indestructible and of a nature that does not perish;
however, it has contact with the material elements.
Therefore, it is not mere consciousness.
Therefore, there is indeed a contradiction.
As for what was said— that "he does not go" is not an injunctive word—
let it not be an injunctive word.
This will be restated as something already understood through another scriptural injunction, namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
